item.title: Police and Army share Ratu Sukuna Bowl after tense 8-8 draw
item.description: Police have retained the Vodafone Ratu Sukuna Bowl for the fifth consecutive year after holding Army to an 8-8 draw in an intense contest, with Army failing to convert a penalty in the dying moments of the match. The two teams will now share the Bowl, with Police, as the current trophy holders, retaining it for the first six months before Army takes over for the next six months.
item.content:encoded:
Police have retained the Vodafone Ratu Sukuna Bowl for the fifth consecutive year after holding Army to an 8-8 draw in an intense contest, with Army failing to convert a penalty in the dying moments of the match.

The two teams will now share the Bowl, with Police, as the current trophy holders, retaining it for the first six months before Army takes over for the next six months.

The Police team received its first red card in the 18th minute, with Sakiusa Vosayaco sent off following a dangerous tackle.

Army kicked off the Vodafone Ratu Sukuna Bowl match, controlling the tempo in the first quarter and scoring a try in the 20th minute to lead 5-0.

Army dominated most of the first half but could not convert much of its territorial advantage into points.

Police made basic errors, which proved costly in the first half, with both teams attempting to play a territorial game.

It was a tense first half, with both sides struggling to find their rhythm.

Army began the second half with disciplinary issues, as their prop was shown a yellow card in the 42nd minute.

Police slowly found their rhythm in the second half and maintained possession during the opening quarter.

They scored their first try in the 50th minute when skipper James Brown won the line-out and led the charge, rumbling all the way to the try line to level the scores at 5-5.

Police were awarded another penalty and opted to kick for goal in the 54th minute, taking an 8-5 lead.

Army levelled the scores at 8-8 after being awarded a penalty in the 63rd minute.

It was an electric finish as Police tried their best to find a winning score, but Army's gutsy defence held firm.

Army were awarded a penalty in the 82nd minute and opted to kick for goal, but failed to convert, allowing Police to retain the Vodafone Ratu Sukuna Bowl for the sixth consecutive year.

item.title: Absenteeism and work ethic issues forcing employers to get foreign workers - Kamikamica
item.description: Our work ethic is deteriorating in Fiji. This has been highlighted by Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica who raised concerns about absenteeism among local workers and businesses opting to hire foreign workers.
item.content:encoded:
Our work ethic is deteriorating in Fiji.

This has been highlighted by Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica who raised concerns about absenteeism among local workers and businesses opting to hire foreign workers.

Kamikamica says some employers are struggling with workers who fail to turn up for work, making it difficult to run their businesses.

He made these comments during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum in Nadi while responding to concerns raised by Chairman of the National Senior Citizens Committee of Fiji, Vineel Nand, about the number of foreign workers in Fiji.

Nand claims there are currently 5,000 illegal foreign workers in the country and questioned why more workers were being sought from Bangladesh when concerns already existed about those working illegally.

He says he has had 23 complaints relating to the issue and had called on political parties to support the local workforce rather than accept more foreign workers.

Responding to Nand, Kamikamica says the issue has been raised repeatedly and the Minister for Immigration is looking into it.

He says he hopes the Immigration Minister will provide an update to the people of Fiji soon.

However, Kamikamica says he had spoken to one of Fiji's largest manufacturers, who told him they would now have to consider hiring foreign workers for the first time.

He says the employer had tried its best to avoid hiring foreign workers but raised absenteeism as a major challenge.

Kamikamica says employees sometimes fail to turn up on Mondays or take Fridays off after receiving their pay on Thursdays.

He says businesses cannot operate under such circumstances and the country needs to have an honest conversation about the issue.

Kamikamica says if employers' concerns about absenteeism are true, people must also take responsibility and address the problem.

He says work should not be treated as an optional exercise, where people choose when they want to turn up.

He adds that this is another long-term issue Fiji needs to address, alongside the breakdown of social structures.

Meanwhile, Nand also raised concerns about the administration of hospitals, saying doctors should not necessarily be responsible for managing hospital administration.

He suggested restructuring hospital management to include professionals with the necessary administrative expertise.

In response, Kamikamica defended the work of the Health Minister, saying the health sector had suffered from years of underinvestment and was facing major challenges, including HIV and non-communicable diseases.

He says the Government has progressively addressed infrastructure issues, including the reopening of Vunisea Hospital and repairs to other hospitals.

Kamikamica says when the Government took office, only three of the eight operating theatres at CWM Hospital were operational, but this has since increased to six.

He says the suggestion about hospital administration is an opinion he respects, but the Health Minister is doing a decent job under difficult circumstances.

Nand clarified that his concerns were not directed at the Minister but at the administration of individual hospitals.

National Federation Party Leader Biman Prasad agreed there was merit in considering a different approach to hospital administration.

Prasad says the proposal to have a hospital services section responsible for administration, while doctors focus on clinical services, was worth exploring.

He says this approach is used in Australia and could help improve the delivery of hospital services in Fiji.

Prasad also acknowledged the work being done to improve health infrastructure, saying the actual delivery of some services still needed further consideration.

Nand also called on political parties to outline their plans for senior citizens and persons with disabilities, highlighting that senior citizens make up nine percent of Fiji's population, while persons with disabilities account for 14 percent.

He urge d businesses to employ at least five percent of persons with disabilities and called for stronger protection of elderly people who transfer their properties to their children but are later neglected or forced out of their homes.

He proposed that property transfers be reversed where children fail to care for their elderly parents.

Responding to the concerns, Next Gen Alliance Deputy Party Leader Noeleen Billings says the party agrees with the issues raised and wants to fast-track reforms through clear performance indicators and timelines .

item.title: President backs national state of disaster declaration, calls for unity in drought response
item.description: The President has backed the declaration of a national state of disaster across Fiji, calling for urgent and coordinated action to address prolonged water shortages, agricultural losses and the growing hardship faced by affected communities. President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu says the declaration announced by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka on Wednesday is an important national response to the ongoi
item.content:encoded:
The President has backed the declaration of a national state of disaster across Fiji, calling for urgent and coordinated action to address prolonged water shortages, agricultural losses and the growing hardship faced by affected communities.

President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu says the declaration announced by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka on Wednesday is an important national response to the ongoing dry spell and the challenges faced by communities across the country.

He says the welfare, safety and well-being of Fijians must remain the priority, particularly during times of hardship and uncertainty.

Lalabalavu says he acknowledges Cabinet's decision, made on the advice of the National Disaster Risk Management Council, to activate the 30-day national disaster arrangements under the National Disaster Risk Management Act 2024.

He also acknowledged the Government's allocation of $20 million towards strengthening emergency assistance, water supplies, agricultural support and other urgent interventions for affected communities.

The President says this is a time for national unity, collective responsibility and decisive action.

He also revealed that he has instructed the National Investment Ceremony scheduled for 24th November to be deferred following the declaration of the national state of disaster.

Lalabalavu is calling on government ministries and agencies, traditional leaders, provincial councils, religious organisations, community leaders, the private sector and development partners to work together in supporting the national response.

He says particular attention must be given to vulnerable families, senior citizens, persons living with disabilities, rural communities and people living in maritime islands who may face additional difficulties accessing safe drinking water and essential services.

The President is also encouraging every Fijian to play their part in conserving water as the country continues to experience the dry spell.

He acknowledged the contribution of farmers to Fiji's food security and economy, and encouraged them to continue working with relevant authorities to ensure assistance reaches those who need it most.

Lalabalavu also recognised the dedication of emergency personnel, civil servants, humanitarian organisations, faith-based organisations and volunteers who continue to serve communities, often under difficult circumstances.

He says Fiji has demonstrated through previous national disasters that its greatest strength lies in unity, resilience, faith and compassion for one another.

The President has assured Fijians of his continued support for all efforts aimed at protecting lives, safeguarding livelihoods and ensuring that no community is left behind.

item.title: Over 5,000 people in Southern Nadi struggle with water shortages, some wait 3 weeks for water trucks
item.description: More than 5,000 people in Nawai, Nawaicoba, Nalovo and surrounding areas in Southern Nadi continue to struggle with unreliable water supply, with some families waiting up to three weeks for water trucks. item.content:encoded:
More than 5,000 people in Nawai, Nawaicoba, Nalovo and surrounding areas in Southern Nadi continue to struggle with unreliable water supply, with some families waiting up to three weeks for water trucks.

This issue has been raised by Nadi resident Viliame Finau, during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum at the FNU Namaka Campus Lecture Theatre in Nadi, saying that residents have been living with water cuts for years, with some having to wait between two and three weeks for water trucks to arrive.

He adds that he regularly interacts with people in these communities and the situation remains the same, with families struggling to access reliable water supply.

Finau says a network of friends is helping deliver water to communities from Nadi towards Sigatoka and Lautoka, but stresses that this cannot continue as a long-term solution.

He says some families are forced to drink salty well water as their usual water sources dry up, while others depend on water deliveries.

Finau recalls visiting a family that tells him they have still not finished the six bottles of water delivered to them a couple of weeks earlier, highlighting how carefully residents are rationing their water.

He also questions Member of Parliament and People First Party representative Rinesh Sharma about the two blue water tanks sitting on the hill at Nawaicoba, asking whether they are established by the previous FijiFirst Government.

Sharma says he entered Parliament in 2022, after FijiFirst lost the election, and cannot comment on what the previous administration did before his time.

However, he says it is the responsibility of the current Government to take forward projects left by the previous administration and ensure they are completed.

Finau then questioned the water supply arrangement involving a pipeline which he says supplies the Marriott Hotel, asking whether water from that main can be intermittently shared with surrounding communities.

He says more than 5,000 people are affected by the shortages and appeals to Government to consider their needs alongside the hotel's water requirements.

Responding to the concerns, Acting Manager Regional Operations Western of the Water Authority of Fiji, Joeli Rabuatoka says the two blue tanks at Nawaicoba are in the final stages of commissioning and are expected to help resolve water supply problems in Southern Nadi.

Rabuatoka explains that the pipeline infrastructure is already in place, but additional storage capacity is needed to cater for the population in the area.

He says the Nadi and Lautoka water systems operate through gravity supply rather than pumping, meaning water needs to be supplied from Nagado towards Nawaicoba to fill the tanks before it can flow by gravity to surrounding communities.

On the concerns about the Marriott Hotel, Rabuatoka says water supply to the hotel is scheduled for two days a week.

He says the Water Authority also considers the needs of surrounding communities and supplements their water supply through water carting.

Rabuatoka says once the two tanks are commissioned and filled, they will provide the additional storage capacity needed to improve water supply to Southern Nadi.

Finau acknowledges the work being carried out by the Water Authority but says feedback from residents indicates that water trucks are not arriving as regularly as they need them to.

He suggests that more water trucks may be required to assist communities while the major water project is being completed.

Finau also raises the possibility of introducing desalination plants in Fiji, particularly for maritime communities, referring to Papua New Guinea's preparations for desalination facilities.

He says he previously visited the District Office to raise the water concerns and contacts the Water Authority, where he is informed that communities will be connected once the major project is completed.

While welcoming the Water Authority's willingness to discuss more regular water carting, Finau maintains his plea for immediate Government intervention.

He is asking Government to consider allowing intermittent sharing of water from the pipeline supplying the Marriott Hotel to help ease the shortages faced by surrounding communities.
